# Decision history — exprim

Every revision of every decision, plus the terminal revisions of other normative records. Includes archived records: this is the project's memory of what it used to think.

## exprim.jbig2.binding-layout

### Revision 1 — jbig2enc-rust bindings: C ABI in jbig2enc-ffi, Python as a sibling crate, core owns a binding-neutral facade

`proposed` · `@exprim.jbig2.binding-layout/1` · scope `path "codecs/jbig2enc-rust/**"`

Expose the codec to non-Rust callers through a separate jbig2enc-ffi crate (library jbig2rs, symbol prefix jbig2rs_). Move the PyO3 binding out of the core crate into its own sibling package. Both bindings sit on one binding-neutral core facade: BilevelImage, EncodeOptions/Preset, DocumentEncoder and ErrorKind.

**Context.** Outside advice proposed a C ABI so that C, C#, Java and Swift callers can use the codec. The core API took only unpacked bytes, used encoders that borrow their config (which rules out an owned C handle), exposed 50+ config fields and flattened every error to a string. Rejected: folding Python into the FFI crate, because the two have different stability contracts and toolchains. Rejected: rebuilding Python on the C ABI, which would lose the buffer protocol, GIL release and real exceptions. Rejected: a jbig2_ prefix, which collides with jbig2dec's exports.

**Consequences.** jbig2enc-rust 0.7.0 drops the python feature, and the PyPI wheel is now built from python/Cargo.toml. Core changes stay additive or deprecations, because Lege tracks git main. No codec logic lives in either binding.

## exprim.jp2.session-buffer-pool

### Revision 1 — JPEG 2000 coefficient and DWT planes reuse one byte-capped pool per session

`proposed` · `@exprim.jp2.session-buffer-pool/1` · scope `path "codecs/jp2lam/src/decode/**"`, `path "codecs/jp2lam/src/dwt/**"`, `path "src/image/jpx.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mod.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/prepared.rs"`

Pool large Tier-1 subband and inverse-DWT planes inside a byte-capped `jp2lam::Jp2BufferPool` (128 MiB default), owned once per `JpxCodec` (`CpuBackend` / `RenderSession`), attached to worker-local `Jp2Decoder`s only for the duration of a decode via an RAII guard, and emptied by `release_idle_memory` or session drop.

**Context.** Fresh allocation and deallocation of multi-megabyte coefficient and DWT prefix planes cost 22-34% of decode wall time on colour scans and up to 50% on grayscale scans on Windows because OS mappings soft-fault on first write and shoot down TLBs on free. Rejected: keeping buffers directly on each thread-local `Jp2Decoder`, which retains up to ~110 MB times the worker thread count after a document closes and cannot be emptied from another thread. Rejected: switching host binaries to `mimalloc`, which was previously disabled in Lege for cross-target build friction, does not benefit library or FFI consumers of `exprim` and `jp2lam`, and holds global OS segments outside `RenderSession::release_idle_memory`. Rejected: leaving fresh allocation in place, which leaves a one-third speedup on scanned books on the table.

**Consequences.** All render workers of a session share one 128 MiB pool cap (matching `SurfacePool`'s ownership model), idle worker threads retain no reference to the pool once a decode returns or unwinds, and `RenderSession::release_idle_memory` drops all parked coefficient planes immediately. Standalone `Jp2Decoder::new()` callers also get a bounded pool automatically and can share one across workers with `Jp2Decoder::with_buffer_pool`. Decoded pixels are bit-identical across all 411 `jp2lam` unit tests, `exprim` integration suites, and five benchmark codestreams.

## exprim.memory.chunked-lowering

### Revision 1 — A page is painted in chunks while it is lowered

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.chunked-lowering/1` · scope `path "src/render_cpu/exec.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mask.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mod.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/prepared.rs"`

CPU rendering no longer lowers a whole page before painting it. Lowering hands the ops lowered so far to the executor whenever 16 MiB of flattened draw geometry is pending, or decoded image samples beyond the image cache's size, and no group or soft-mask scope is open; the ops are painted and dropped and only clip geometry is kept. The page surface is allocated when the first chunk is painted.

**Context.** Lowering flattened every stroke outline and decoded every image before the first pixel: 84 MB of points beside a 135 MB surface on a stroke-dense map at 600 dpi, and every image of a page at once. Rejected: a resumable lowerer (the loop is 700 lines over twenty locals and is shared with tiling cells, attribution and the GPU seam; a sink called from inside the loop leaves it one loop); expanding strokes lazily at paint time (expansion would run twice, once for bounds, on the path the renderer work has been speeding up); flushing on image bytes at the geometry threshold (measured 21 MB worse on a scan page: the images stay in the image cache anyway, and the flush only brought the surface into existence beside the next image's decode); allocating the surface before lowering (the same cost on every image page).

**Consequences.** The ops, their order and their geometry are those of one-pass lowering: unit tests compare a flush after every op, a few flushes and none with the one-pass executor, and the page-hash gate is unchanged with the chunk size forced to zero. Stroke fixture at 600 dpi: 218 to 162 MB. A flush cannot happen inside a group or soft-mask scope, so a page that is one large group lowers in one piece as before. Clip geometry is compacted and its ranges rewritten at each flush. A mask whose clip is still on the clip stack survives the chunk boundary. Lowering time in the profile is what remains after subtracting the painting done inside it. The prepared-page profiling entry and the GPU seam still lower in one piece.

## exprim.memory.clip-mask-store

### Revision 1 — Clip masks live in a planned per-page store: shared, released after last use, held under a budget

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.clip-mask-store/1` · scope `path "src/render_cpu/exec.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mask.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/prepared.rs"`

A page's clip masks are owned by one store (ClipMasks). Lowering points a path clip at an earlier clip when both have bit-identical device geometry, the same fill rule and envelope, and the same mask above them. The executor drops each mask after the last op that consumes it, keeps the resident ones under a budget of eight page-sized coverage planes (at least 64 MiB) by evicting the least recently used, and on pages with sixteen or more masks builds ahead in budget-sized parallel batches in first-use order.

**Context.** Every consumed mask used to be built before the draw loop and held until the page ended, by four draw paths that each cached into a bare vector. A 55 KB page with one page-sized clip re-established 200 times held 3.47 GB of masks at 600 dpi beside a 135 MB surface, outside RenderLimits.max_page_bytes, outside the scheduler estimate and invisible to peak_live_bytes. Rejected: release after last use alone (deeply nested distinct clips stay unbounded); failing the page past a byte limit (it renders correctly today, only expensively); run-length masks (every consumer indexes the plane directly, and it would not help distinct dense masks); sharing at execution time (the duplicate geometry could not be reclaimed from the arena).

**Consequences.** A mask is a pure function of the prepared page, so sharing, eviction and rebuild cannot change a byte; unit tests compare the planned, zero-budget and unshared paths, and the page-hash gate is unchanged. A page that keeps more than a budget of large masks in use at once (nested distinct page-sized clips more than eight deep) rebuilds a mask when it returns to it: bounded extra time in exchange for bounded memory. The parallel build is at most a budget wide, so fewer than one mask per core when masks are page-sized. Sharing stops after four distinct clips collide on one geometry hash, because the hash input comes from the document. PDF_RENDERER_CLIPSHARE and PDF_RENDERER_CLIPMASK_MB isolate the two halves on one binary. The scheduler's job estimate still does not include the mask budget.

## exprim.memory.reorder-backlog-bytes

### Revision 1 — The scheduler bounds the reorder backlog in bytes by gating when out-of-order pages start

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.reorder-backlog-bytes/1` · scope `path "src/render_scheduler/**"`

Finished pages waiting for in-order emission are bounded in bytes (256 MiB by default) as well as by the page-count window. Render workers take the lowest-numbered compiled page from an ordered ready set and do not start a page that would finish out of order while the backlog plus its surface exceeds the limit; the page the collector needs next is always accepted and always started.

**Context.** The permit is released when a render returns and the only bound on finished pages was the window of four per worker, so a slow early page or a slow emit callback held 79 finished surfaces: 2.6 GB at 300 dpi while 0.4 GB of the 4 GiB budget was in use. Rejected: admitting by bytes in the feeder (it admits pages before they are compiled and cannot know their size); keeping the permit until emission (the measured backlog fits under the budget, so it would not bind, and it needs a head-of-line reservation inside the budget); a bounded result channel (deadlocks when workers finish ahead of the head).

**Consequences.** The backlog can exceed the limit by the pages already rendering when it was reached, at most one surface per render worker. Small pages never wait on it: the default holds 32 Letter surfaces at 2x, the window the short-document throughput measurement settled on. Measured on a 200-page document with a slow first page: 688 MiB at 300 dpi instead of 2,616 MiB, wall time unchanged. Throughput on real large-page documents was not measured. Output order, per-page results and cancellation draining are unchanged.

## exprim.memory.session-bounds

### Revision 1 — Session memory is bounded per document by explicit options; RGB can be packed in place on request

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.session-bounds/1` · scope `path "src/reader/page_cache.rs"`, `path "src/reader/session.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mod.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/surface.rs"`

A session's compiled-page cache is bounded in bytes as well as by count, and the bounds of that cache, the image, font and glyph caches and the buffer pool are set per session. A separate render call packs RGB inside the surface it was rendered on; the default call still returns an exactly sized buffer. The buffer pool keeps only the three most recently parked sizes.

**Context.** Eight compiled pages of full-resolution image samples sat behind a count of eight; cache budgets were constants; and the session's RGB output held the RGBA surface and an RGB copy together (241 MB for a 600 dpi page). In-place packing could not replace the default: callers and tests in this repository and its consumers rely on the pixel buffer being exactly stride times height, and a caller that retains many rasters would hold a third more. The pool's size rule came from a measurement: with one buffer per distinct size, eight pages of a scanned book whose pages all differ kept 150 MB parked where the old three slots kept 57 MB.

**Consequences.** Export and print, which drop the raster after use, call the in-place form: four bytes per pixel at the peak instead of seven. A host with many documents open divides its allowance through the options; there is still no cap shared across sessions. A compiled page heavier than the whole byte budget is kept alone rather than recompiled on every use. Page weight is an estimate dominated by image samples and encoded payloads; font programs, shared by the document, are not counted.

## exprim.memory.session-owned-idle-memory

### Revision 1 — Reusable buffers and worker contexts belong to the backend and the session, not to threads

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.session-owned-idle-memory/1` · scope `path "src/reader/session.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mod.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/surface.rs"`

Finished page buffers kept for reuse live in one pool per CpuBackend, capped at 256 MiB, used by renders through a caller-owned worker context. RenderSession keeps its parse and raster contexts in a checkout list it owns. Both are dropped with the session and can be released earlier with RenderSession::release_idle_memory. RenderSession::open_path maps the file.

**Context.** Each worker context parked one page buffer of any size, a thread-local kept two more sizes up to 128 MiB each, and the session's contexts were thread-locals reset only when the thread next served another session. Nothing capped the total and closing a document freed none of it on the pool threads that had worked on it: twenty threads at 300 dpi kept about 670 MB parked, plus each thread's parse cache. Rejected: per-thread slots keyed by session (still thread count times page size, and unreachable from another thread on drop); no reuse at all (the 2026-09-04 measurement shows fresh mappings dominate scan pages).

**Consequences.** While the pool is under its cap any thread reuses any free buffer, which is at least the hit rate the per-thread slots gave. When many threads render pages too large for the cap, some renders allocate a fresh surface: slower, never different. The one-shot path the scheduler uses is deliberately not pooled, as it retained nothing before. Rendering RGB8 through the session still holds the RGBA surface and the packed RGB plane together (7 bytes per pixel at that instant); removing that needs RGB-native or banded rendering. A context whose job panics is dropped instead of returned.

## exprim.memory.shared-image-samples

### Revision 1 — Filter-decoded image samples decode once per overlapping compile, into one exactly-sized buffer

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.shared-image-samples/1` · scope `path "src/content/interpret.rs"`, `path "src/document/**"`, `path "src/structure/decode.rs"`, `path "src/structure/predictor.rs"`

Samples of Flate, LZW, RunLength and raw image streams are decoded into one buffer of the size the image dictionary implies, and page compiles that overlap in time share one decoded copy of an image object through a document-scoped cache that holds entries only while a compile is running.

**Context.** These images are decoded by the page compiler, not by a backend codec, so the renderer's image cache never saw them: each page compile inflated its own copy into a doubling buffer, copied it again into its final allocation, and carried it until its render finished. One 57 MiB image peaked at 123 MiB; sixty pages sharing it peaked at 725 MiB. Rejected: moving the decode into the renderer behind the image cache (changes the IR contract and every consumer of image samples); weak cache entries (a weak reference to a shared slice keeps the whole allocation); keying by object id alone (the same id can resolve to a different body or filter parameters on another worker in edge cases, so a hit also matches a fingerprint of both).

**Consequences.** A size hint commits only when the stream ends cleanly at exactly the hinted length and otherwise the previous path runs unchanged, so truncated, over-long and corrupt streams produce the bytes and errors they did before; a truncated image briefly allocates the hinted size. A hit charges the decode budget what the publishing decode charged. Two compiles separated by a moment with no compile running do not share. Compiled pages waiting in the scheduler queue or the session's page cache still carry full-resolution samples, and text extraction still decodes images it does not use; removing those needs the decode moved out of the compiler.

## exprim.memory.strip-output

### Revision 1 — Large pages are rendered in strips: Gray8 and RGB always, RGBA when offscreens are large

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.strip-output/1` · scope `path "src/content/lower.rs"`, `path "src/page_ir/mod.rs"`, `path "src/reader/session.rs"`, `path "src/render_api/mod.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/exec.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/image.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/mod.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/prepared.rs"`, `path "src/render_cpu/surface.rs"`, `path "src/render_scheduler/mod.rs"`

A page whose RGBA surface would exceed twice the strip target (32 MiB by default) is rendered as horizontal strips when that pays. For an output converted from the surface (Gray8, or RGB through the backend's RGB calls and RenderSession::render and render_in_place) it always pays: each strip is converted into its rows of an exact-length output buffer and the whole surface never exists. For RGBA output it pays only when the page's transparency-group and soft-mask intermediates would themselves exceed twice the target at page size; the strips are then copied into the page. Each strip is a complete lower-and-paint pass in the page's own device coordinates with painting clamped to the strip's rows. The scheduler budgets a job for what the backend says it paints on.

**Context.** Every unbounded intermediate of a page was proportional to its pixel count: the RGBA surface, the plane converted beside it, group and soft-mask offscreens, tiling fills. A strip cannot be a translated crop, because f32 transforms are not translation-invariant and output must stay byte-identical. Three costs had to go first, each measured with strips forced: every op lowered once per strip (fixed by recording, in the first strip, the rows each op emits and skipping ops that miss a later strip); a Gray8 image expanded whole per strip (now only the rows a draw reads, CMYK likewise); an image decoded again per strip when the shared cache cannot hold it (the render keeps it until its last row). Rejected: surfaces in the output format (every span and image kernel once per format, and groups still need alpha); banding inside groups only (no gain for the page surface); keeping the lowered page across strips (brings back the whole-page geometry arena); engaging at the target itself (a 300 dpi Letter page is 32.1 MiB and would split in two for a small saving on the commonest size); strips for every large RGBA page (an RGBA page is its own surface, so strips add a buffer and a copy unless offscreens shrink by more). The RGBA rule needed an honest offscreen figure: the page complexity counted wrapper groups that the backend paints straight onto their parent, which would have sent most large RGBA pages into strips for nothing, and counted soft masks not at all. For the scheduler, rejected: reading the strip size from a constant in the estimate (a backend configured otherwise would be under-charged); the estimate takes the plane from the backend through a trait method whose default is the whole surface. For clip masks, rejected: clamping a clip's envelope to the strip (draw bounds are cut by the envelope before the strip's rows, and the first strip records each op's rows from them for the other strips to cull by, so a clamped envelope would record the first strip's rows for everything under a clip); a clip carries a separate mask extent instead.

**Consequences.** At 600 dpi Letter a text page peaks at 67 MB as Gray8 (175 before) and 134 MB as RGB (242); a page with tilings, groups and a soft mask at 94 MB as Gray8 and 202 MB as RGBA (309 both before). Wall time on the pages measured is within -37% and +10% of one pass; pages under the threshold, and RGBA pages without large offscreens, are unchanged. Every strip uses a surface of the same height, the last using its top rows, so one buffer serves the page and the pool; a shorter last strip leaked one buffer into the pool per render. RenderStats counts each strip's work; surface_bytes is the strip for converted output and the page for RGBA. The render and the scheduler's estimate take the strip choice from one function (CpuBackend::strip_rows_for); they must not be allowed to diverge, or jobs are under-charged. With the strip charge, 32 Gray8 pages at 600 dpi under a 256 MiB budget went from 2.8 s to 1.2 s on one document and 7.6 s to 6.8 s on another, and the process holds 25 to 65 MiB more at that budget because the budget is now filled by real jobs. PageComplexity gained soft-mask and tiling figures and stopped counting directly painted groups; the direct-paint condition is mirrored from render_cpu::exec and must follow it. A strip builds each clip mask over its own rows (PreparedClip::mask_bounds); PreparedClip::bounds must stay the whole envelope. A page of 500 clipped forms at 600 dpi as Gray8 went from 122 MB to 81 MB. Tiling fills keep full bounds and are not bounded by the strip. The mask budget and the estimate's charge for clip masks and tiling fills are still at page size. PDF_RENDERER_STRIP_ROWS forces strips at any size and format so the page-hash gate can exercise them on small pages; it must keep working.

## exprim.memory.wrapper-groups-direct

### Revision 1 — An opaque non-isolated wrapper group paints on its parent surface

`proposed` · `@exprim.memory.wrapper-groups-direct/1` · scope `path "src/render_cpu/exec.rs"`

A transparency group that is non-isolated, Normal blend, opacity 255, not knockout, with no soft mask in force at its invocation, and whose bounds lie inside its parent surface, runs its ops on the parent surface. Every other group keeps its offscreen.

**Context.** Such a group was rendered on an offscreen seeded with a copy of the parent's pixels and then copied back row by row (composite_group_seeded at opacity 255 without a mask is a copy). Group bounds are the union of the content's op bounds and every op is confined to its own bounds, so painting in place writes the same bytes to the same pixels. This is the wrapper most producers put around a page or a form; at 600 dpi it cost a second 135 MB surface and two full copies. A test-only switch keeps the offscreen path as the reference, following the tile-culling test.

**Consequences.** Peak for a page-sized wrapper at 600 dpi fell from 260 MB to 140 MB and warm render cycles by about a fifth on the group fixture. Isolated groups, groups with constant alpha below one, non-Normal group blends, knockout groups and groups under a soft mask are unchanged; an exact elision for those is not known (8-bit rounding differs when a group is composited as a unit). A cancelled render may now have painted part of the group onto the page surface; cancelled surfaces are discarded, so nothing observes it.

## exprim.structure.rebuild-skips-stream-bodies

### Revision 1 — The cross-reference rebuild scan steps over stream bodies whose /Length is verified

`proposed` · `@exprim.structure.rebuild-skips-stream-bodies/1` · scope `path "src/structure/loader.rs"`

When the full-file rebuild finds an object header, it checks whether the object is a dictionary followed by a stream whose /Length is a direct number landing on endstream, and if so resumes scanning after the body instead of reading it. A stream whose /Length is missing, indirect or wrong is scanned byte by byte as before.

**Context.** The four largest local scans have a startxref a few kilobytes short of the real table. The loader finds the table by its keyword, sees that its offsets are stale, and rebuilds, as PDFium does. The rebuild compared every byte of the file against four keywords: 3.3 s for a 781 MB file, and every page of the memory map resident before the first page was rendered, though the file's dictionaries are a few megabytes and the rest is image data. Rejected: repairing each stale offset by a local search instead of rebuilding (the existing rule, and PDFium, never trust a table found by scanning whose offsets miss; it would also change which revision of an object wins); a faster substring search (still reads everything); reading through a bounded window instead of the map (same bytes read, and no help to callers that hold the file in memory). The skip condition is the object parser's own condition for taking /Length at its word, so what is skipped is exactly what every later read of that object treats as opaque data.

**Consequences.** Measured: open of the 781 MB file 3,286 ms to 15 ms, working set after open 787 MB to 14 MB; the other three likewise (585 to 14, 298 to 9, 244 to 8 MB). Page hashes of those documents are unchanged. Behaviour differs in one deliberate way: bytes inside a verified stream body that look like an object header, an object-stream or xref-stream marker or a trailer are no longer indexed, where before an uncompressed embedded PDF could displace real objects (last occurrence wins). An object hidden inside a stream with a correct /Length is by definition stream data. Each object header now costs one extra dictionary parse during a rebuild. The backward search for the xref keyword when startxref misses is unchanged and still reads the whole file when no classic table exists.
